title: CUET Political Science Test 12
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Country with a quarter of the world's oil reserves
questions.question: Which country, according to NCERT, holds about a quarter of the world's oil reserves?
options: A) Saudi Arabia
B) Venezuela
C) United States
D) Kazakhstan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Saudi Arabia
Why: NCERT says Saudi Arabia holds about a quarter of the world's total reserves.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) hold smaller shares.
Key point: The Gulf is central to oil geopolitics.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Where the CPI's early support lay
questions.question: In the early years after independence, the CPI's support was concentrated mainly in:
options: A) Rajasthan, Gujarat and Punjab
B) Assam, Manipur and Tripura
C) Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi
D) Andhra, West Bengal, Bihar and Kerala
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Andhra, West Bengal, Bihar and Kerala
Why: NCERT says the CPI's support was concentrated in Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Bihar and Kerala.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) were not its main areas; the Jana Sangh's base lay partly in (A) and (C).
Key point: Communist strength was regional.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Aim of the militants in Punjab
questions.question: During the 1980s, militant groups in Punjab demanded:
options: A) the merger of Punjab with Haryana
B) a Hindi-speaking State in Punjab
C) a separate country called Khalistan
D) the return of the Indian capital to Lahore
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) a separate country called Khalistan
Why: Militant groups demanded a separate Sikh nation called Khalistan.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were not their demands.
Key point: Militancy grew after the failure of moderate politics in Punjab.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Asia from 1953 to 1994, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The ASEAN Regional Forum is set up
(B) India and China restore full diplomatic relations
(C) The Korean War comes to an end
(D) India launches its Look East policy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: (C) The Korean War ended in 1953. (B) India and China restored full ties in 1976. (D) The Look East policy began in 1991. (A) The ARF was set up in 1994.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts 1976 before 1953. Option (C) puts the Look East policy before 1976. Option (D) puts the ARF before the Look East policy.
Key point: 1953 → 1976 → 1991 → 1994.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Groups to whom 'garibi hatao' appealed
questions.question: The slogan 'garibi hatao' in 1971 was aimed especially at winning the support of:
options: A) big industrialists, bankers and the former princes
B) the landless, Dalits, Adivasis and the young unemployed
C) foreign investors and the large multinational firms
D) members of the Syndicate and their followers in the party
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) the landless, Dalits, Adivasis and the young unemployed
Why: The slogan sought support from the disadvantaged: landless labourers, Dalits, Adivasis, minorities, women and the unemployed youth.
Why not the others:
(A) Princes lost their privy purses.
(C) The slogan was aimed at Indian voters.
(D) The Syndicate opposed Indira Gandhi.
Key point: Indira Gandhi built a new social base among the poor.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: How the IAEA checks nuclear facilities
questions.question: How does the International Atomic Energy Agency try to ensure that nuclear reactors are used for peaceful purposes?
options: A) By running all the world's reactors itself
B) By fixing the price of uranium each year
C) By sending UN troops to nuclear-weapon states
D) By regularly inspecting nuclear facilities
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) By regularly inspecting nuclear facilities
Why: IAEA inspectors regularly visit nuclear facilities to check that they are used for peaceful purposes.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not its functions.
Key point: The IAEA promotes peaceful use of nuclear energy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: How far Indian forces advanced in 1965
questions.question: During the war of 1965, Indian forces advanced close to which city?
options: A) Karachi
B) Dhaka
C) Lahore
D) Kabul
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lahore
Why: NCERT notes that Indian troops reached close to Lahore in 1965.
Why not the others:
(A) Karachi was not reached.
(B) Dhaka was the focus of the 1971 war.
(D) Kabul is in Afghanistan.
Key point: The war ended with the Tashkent Agreement.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: A downside of China's reforms
questions.question: Which of the following is a negative outcome of China's economic reforms, according to NCERT?
options: A) A fall in foreign investment
B) A collapse of farm output
C) A rise in unemployment
D) The end of foreign trade
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A rise in unemployment
Why: NCERT notes that unemployment has risen, along with problems like environmental damage and corruption.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are wrong; investment, farm output and trade all grew.
Key point: Rapid growth brought new problems.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Leaders in India's foreign relations, 1950s–1960s
questions.question:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Role).

List-I
(A) V.K. Krishna Menon
(B) Alexei Kosygin
(C) Zhou Enlai
(D) Homi J. Bhabha

List-II
(I) Led India's nuclear programme in its early years
(II) Soviet Prime Minister who brought India and Pakistan together at Tashkent
(III) Chinese Premier during the years of 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'
(IV) India's Defence Minister during the war of 1962
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: Krishna Menon was Defence Minister in 1962 (IV). Kosygin mediated at Tashkent (II). Zhou Enlai was China's Premier in the friendship years (III). Bhabha led the early nuclear programme (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Menon and Kosygin. Option (C) swaps Kosygin and Zhou Enlai. Option (D) swaps Zhou Enlai and Bhabha.
Key point: Diplomacy, war and science all shaped India's external relations.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: A result of the Chinese takeover of Tibet
questions.question: Which of the following followed China's takeover of Tibet and the uprising of 1959?
options: A) Tibet was given a seat in the United Nations.
B) Large numbers of Tibetans took refuge in India.
C) India and China signed a defence alliance.
D) Tibet was merged with the Indian State of Assam.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Large numbers of Tibetans took refuge in India.
Why: The Dalai Lama and many Tibetans fled to India, which gave them refuge; this angered China.
Why not the others:
(A) Tibet has no UN seat.
(C) Relations worsened instead.
(D) Tibet was never merged with India.
Key point: Tibet was a source of tension between India and China.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Aftermath of the demolition at Ayodhya
questions.question: What followed the demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya in December 1992?
options: A) The two communities signed a lasting agreement.
B) Communal clashes broke out in many parts of India.
C) The Ayodhya dispute was settled within a week.
D) The BJP withdrew from politics altogether.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Communal clashes broke out in many parts of India.
Why: The demolition was followed by communal violence in many parts of the country.
Why not the others:
(A) No agreement followed.
(C) The dispute continued for many years.
(D) The BJP remained a major party.
Key point: The demolition deepened the debate on secularism.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Commons, ozone and indigenous rights — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Common property resources in India have declined because of privatisation and population growth.
(B) The Montreal Protocol was about cutting carbon dioxide emissions.
(C) The UN set up a Working Group on Indigenous Populations in 1982.
(D) Antarctica is the world's largest wilderness area.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) (A) only
B) (B) only
C) (C) only
D) (D) only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: the Montreal Protocol dealt with ozone-depleting substances, not carbon dioxide.
Why not the others: (A) commons have shrunk through privatisation and other pressures. (C) the Working Group was set up in 1982. (D) Antarctica is the largest wilderness. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Different treaties tackle different environmental problems.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Not part of the Soviet bloc
questions.question: Which of the following countries was NOT part of the Soviet bloc in Eastern Europe?
options: A) Spain
B) Poland
C) Hungary
D) Bulgaria
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Spain
Why: Spain is in Western Europe and was never in the Soviet bloc.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) were part of the Soviet bloc.
Key point: The Soviet bloc fell apart in 1989.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Not among the developments of the late 1980s and early 1990s
questions.question: NCERT lists several developments that shaped politics around 1990. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
options: A) The end of the Congress system in 1989
B) The rise of the Mandal issue
C) The proclamation of an Emergency
D) The start of new economic policies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The proclamation of an Emergency
Why: The Emergency was proclaimed in 1975, not around 1990.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D), along with Rajiv Gandhi's assassination and the Ayodhya issue, are the developments NCERT lists.
Key point: Several changes came together to transform politics after 1989.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Ideological effect of the Soviet collapse
questions.question: What did the end of the Soviet Union mean for the ideological contest of the Cold War years?
options: A) Communism became the dominant ideology worldwide.
B) The contest grew sharper between the two blocs.
C) Every country adopted the Soviet constitution.
D) The rivalry between socialism and capitalism ended.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The rivalry between socialism and capitalism ended.
Why: With the Soviet collapse, the ideological contest between socialism and capitalism ended, and capitalism became dominant.
Why not the others:
(A) Communism declined.
(B) The Soviet bloc no longer existed.
(C) No country adopted the Soviet constitution.
Key point: 1991 ended the Cold War rivalry.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: States of the North-East and Goa
questions.question:
Match List-I (State) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Arunachal Pradesh
(B) Tripura
(C) Meghalaya
(D) Goa

List-II
(I) Carved out of Assam as a separate State in 1972
(II) Earlier known as NEFA, it became a State in 1987
(III) An opinion poll in 1967 rejected its merger with Maharashtra
(IV) Its original inhabitants were reduced to a minority by migration
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Arunachal, once NEFA, became a State in 1987 (II). Tripura's original inhabitants became a minority (IV). Meghalaya was carved out of Assam in 1972 (I). Goa's opinion poll rejected merger (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Arunachal and Tripura. Option (C) swaps Tripura and Meghalaya. Option (D) swaps Meghalaya and Goa.
Key point: The map of the North-East was redrawn several times.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of sustainable development
questions.question: Sustainable development means development that:
options: A) uses up all resources quickly in order to grow fast
B) is limited only to the rich industrialised countries
C) meets today's needs without harming the future
D) stops all industrial activity everywhere in the world
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) meets today's needs without harming the future
Why: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) misstate the idea.
Key point: The idea was popularised by the Brundtland Report.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Why India's leaders chose planning
questions.question: Why did India's leaders after independence favour economic planning?
options: A) Because the British had left a plan for them to follow
B) Because the Constitution banned private businesses
C) Because India had no agriculture to speak of in 1947
D) Because they saw the state as key to ending poverty
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because they saw the state as key to ending poverty
Why: The leaders believed the state had to play a key role in removing poverty and building the economy.
Why not the others:
(A) No such plan existed.
(B) Private business was allowed.
(C) Agriculture was the mainstay of the economy.
Key point: Planning reflected faith in the state as an agent of development.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Plans, the Planning Commission and liberalisation — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Second Five Year Plan sought to bring about a quick structural change in the economy.
(B) The Planning Commission was abolished by the Janata government in 1977.
(C) From the 1990s India moved away from the Nehruvian model towards liberalisation.
(D) Operation Flood linked rural milk producers with consumers in the cities.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) (A) only
B) (B) only
C) (C) only
D) (D) only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: the Planning Commission continued until 2015, when NITI Aayog replaced it.
Why not the others: (A) the Second Plan aimed at quick structural transformation. (C) liberalisation marked a shift from the earlier model. (D) Operation Flood connected villages to urban markets. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Planning gave way to liberalisation from 1991.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Parties of the 1950s — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The CPI had a well-organised party machinery and dedicated workers.
(B) The Jana Sangh drew its support mainly from urban areas in north India.
(C) The Swatantra Party's support came largely from industrialists and big landlords.
(D) The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934 as a rival party outside the Congress.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) (A) and (B) only
B) (B), (C) and (D) only
C) (A), (B) and (C) only
D) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the CPI had an organised machinery and committed cadre. (B) the Jana Sangh's base was mainly urban and north Indian. (C) the Swatantra Party appealed to industrialists, zamindars and princes.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the CSP was formed within the Congress by younger leaders. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Each opposition party had a distinct social base.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Interim agreement signed by the Nizam
questions.question: In November 1947, the Nizam of Hyderabad entered into a ________ Agreement with India, while negotiations continued.
options: A) Standstill
B) Tashkent
C) Simla
D) Panchsheel
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Standstill
Why: The Nizam signed a Standstill Agreement with India for a year while he negotiated.
Why not the others:
(B) Tashkent concerns 1966.
(C) The Simla Agreement was signed in 1972.
(D) Panchsheel was agreed with China in 1954.
Key point: The Standstill Agreement only delayed Hyderabad's integration.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Groups in the Congress's social coalition
questions.question: Why does NCERT describe the Congress of the 1950s as a social coalition?
options: A) It brought together peasants, industrialists, workers and many castes.
B) It was made up only of the urban, English-speaking middle class.
C) It was an alliance of regional parties from every State of India.
D) It drew its support only from the big landowners of the countryside.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It brought together peasants, industrialists, workers and many castes.
Why: The Congress included peasants and industrialists, villagers and city dwellers, workers and owners, and middle, low and high castes.
Why not the others:
(B) Its base was far wider.
(C) It was one party, not an alliance of regional parties.
(D) Landowners were only one part of its support.
Key point: Its broad base made the Congress hard to challenge.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: China, Japan and ASEAN — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Both India and China are nuclear powers.
(B) China attracted foreign investment through Special Economic Zones.
(C) ASEAN has set up a Free Trade Area among its members.
(D) Japan is a permanent member of the UN Security Council.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) (A) and (C) only
B) (A), (B) and (C) only
C) (B), (C) and (D) only
D) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) India and China both have nuclear weapons. (B) SEZs drew foreign investment into China. (C) ASEAN created the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA).
Why not the others: (D) is false: Japan is not a permanent member, though it is a major contributor to the UN budget. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (B).
Key point: Japan's economic weight is not matched by a permanent seat.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Why India's leaders chose a secular state after Partition
questions.question: Why did India's leaders insist, after Partition, that India would be a secular state?
options: A) Because all Muslims had migrated to Pakistan in 1947
B) Because the British had ordered them to remain secular
C) Because every citizen was to have equal rights
D) Because religion had played no part in the Partition
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because every citizen was to have equal rights
Why: Despite Partition on religious lines, the leaders were committed to a state that treated all citizens equally, whatever their religion.
Why not the others:
(A) A large Muslim population remained in India.
(B) The British gave no such order.
(D) Religion was central to Partition.
Key point: Secularism was a response to, not a result of, Partition.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Why the Janata government did not last
questions.question: Why did the Janata government formed in 1977 fall within about two years?
options: A) It lacked direction and its leaders fought over power.
B) The Supreme Court declared its election invalid.
C) It was dismissed by the President under Article 356.
D) The Congress joined it and then took over the cabinet.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It lacked direction and its leaders fought over power.
Why: The Janata Party lacked a common programme and its leaders, such as Morarji Desai and Charan Singh, competed for power, so the government collapsed.
Why not the others:
(B) No court invalidated its election.
(C) Article 356 concerns State governments.
(D) The Congress did not join it.
Key point: Opposition unity built on anti-Emergency sentiment was fragile.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Sikkim's place among the States
questions.question: In 1975 Sikkim became the ________ State of the Indian Union.
options: A) 17th
B) 25th
C) 20th
D) 22nd
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 22nd
Why: Sikkim became the 22nd State of India in 1975.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) do not match NCERT.
Key point: Sikkim's merger ended its monarchy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: UN reforms agreed in 2005
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Human Rights Council
(B) Peacebuilding Commission
(C) Democracy Fund
(D) Millennium Development Goals

List-II
(I) A body to help countries recover after conflict
(II) A body set up in 2006 to protect human rights
(III) A fund to support democracy around the world
(IV) Agreed targets for reducing poverty and improving health and education
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: The Human Rights Council was set up in 2006 (II). The Peacebuilding Commission helps countries after conflict (I). The Democracy Fund supports democracy (III). The MDGs set development targets (IV).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the Council and the Commission. Option (C) swaps the Commission and the Fund. Option (D) swaps the Fund and the MDGs.
Key point: The 2005 summit brought several new UN bodies and goals.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: EU members' split over Iraq
questions.question: What did the US invasion of Iraq in 2003 show about the European Union?
options: A) The EU sent a joint army to fight alongside the US.
B) The EU unanimously condemned the US and cut off trade.
C) The EU's members agreed to leave NATO together.
D) Its members were divided, with Britain backing the US.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Its members were divided, with Britain backing the US.
Why: Britain backed the US, while Germany and France opposed the invasion, showing that EU members did not always speak with one voice.
Why not the others:
(A) There was no joint EU army.
(B) The members were divided.
(C) No member left NATO over this.
Key point: The EU's foreign policy is limited by national differences.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Concepts of non-traditional security
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Human security
(B) Global threats
(C) Terrorism
(D) Cooperative security

List-II
(I) Political violence that deliberately targets civilians
(II) Working with other states, NGOs and international bodies
(III) Protection of people rather than of states
(IV) Problems like global warming that affect every country
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Human security protects people rather than states (III). Global threats affect every country (IV). Terrorism targets civilians (I). Cooperative security involves many partners (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps human security and global threats. Option (B) swaps global threats and terrorism. Option (C) swaps terrorism and cooperative security.
Key point: Non-traditional security widens who and what is protected.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Who carries out terrorism
questions.question: Unlike traditional military threats, terrorism is usually carried out by:
options: A) the regular armies of rival states
B) groups that are not states
C) the UN Security Council
D) international trade bodies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) groups that are not states
Why: Terrorism is political violence by groups, not by states' regular armies.
Why not the others:
(A) Armies of states represent traditional threats.
(C) and (D) do not carry out violence.
Key point: Non-state threats are harder to deter.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Politics from 1989 to 2014 — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) After Rajiv Gandhi's assassination, P.V. Narasimha Rao became Congress leader and Prime Minister.
(B) The Janata Dal, formed in 1988, was led by V.P. Singh.
(C) Between 1989 and 2014, no single party won a majority of its own in the Lok Sabha.
(D) The United Front government of 1996 was led by Atal Bihari Vajpayee.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) (A), (B) and (C) only
B) (A) and (C) only
C) (B), (C) and (D) only
D) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Rao became PM in 1991. (B) V.P. Singh led the Janata Dal. (C) from 1989 until 2014 no party won a majority alone.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the United Front was led by H.D. Deve Gowda and then I.K. Gujral; Vajpayee led the BJP. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (B) leaves out (B).
Key point: Coalition governments dominated for a quarter of a century.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Ending of the USSR — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Gorbachev tried to improve relations with the West.
(B) Soviet citizens came to know how far the West had advanced, which fed discontent.
(C) The Soviet Union was dissolved by a resolution of the UN General Assembly.
(D) Russia, Ukraine and Belarus took the lead in ending the USSR and forming the CIS.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) (A) only
B) (B) only
C) (C) only
D) (D) only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the USSR was dissolved by its own republics' leaders, not by the UN.
Why not the others: (A) Gorbachev sought to normalise ties with the West. (B) awareness of Western progress fed discontent. (D) Russia, Ukraine and Belarus led the move to the CIS. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The USSR was dissolved from within.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Outside power with a strategic partnership with Pakistan
questions.question: Which outside power, an important player in South Asia, has a close strategic partnership with Pakistan?
options: A) Japan
B) Brazil
C) Australia
D) China
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) China
Why: NCERT notes China's strategic partnership with Pakistan as a key factor in South Asian politics.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not described this way.
Key point: Outside powers shape the region's politics.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why the Congress won a record majority in 1984
questions.question: What mainly explains the Congress's record victory in the Lok Sabha election of 1984?
options: A) The merger of the BJP with the Congress
B) A wave of sympathy after Indira Gandhi's assassination
C) The implementation of the Mandal Commission report
D) The economic reforms started in the previous year
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A wave of sympathy after Indira Gandhi's assassination
Why: Indira Gandhi's assassination in October 1984 created a wave of sympathy that gave the Congress, led by Rajiv Gandhi, a huge majority.
Why not the others:
(A) No such merger happened.
(C) Mandal was implemented in 1990.
(D) The reforms began in 1991.
Key point: 1984 was the Congress's last single-party majority for decades.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: What Mujib did to Bangladesh's party system
questions.question: What did Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman do after amending Bangladesh's Constitution in 1975?
options: A) He handed power to the army at once.
B) He made Bangladesh a monarchy under his family.
C) He abolished all parties except his own Awami League.
D) He merged Bangladesh back into Pakistan.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He abolished all parties except his own Awami League.
Why: Mujib shifted to a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League; he was assassinated later that year.
Why not the others:
(A) The army took over only after his assassination.
(B) Bangladesh was never a monarchy.
(D) Bangladesh remained independent.
Key point: Bangladesh soon moved away from its democratic start.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Not among the proposed criteria for a permanent seat
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the criteria proposed for new permanent members of the Security Council?
options: A) Being a major economic power
B) Making a large contribution to the UN budget
C) Possessing nuclear weapons
D) Respecting democracy and human rights
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Possessing nuclear weapons
Why: Having nuclear weapons is not among the proposed criteria.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D), along with military power, population and representation of diversity, are among the criteria discussed.
Key point: There is no agreement on who deserves a permanent seat.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: What the Tamil militants called their homeland
questions.question: The separate state demanded by Tamil militants in Sri Lanka was called:
options: A) Eelam
B) Kandy
C) Jaffna Pradesh
D) Lanka Desh
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Eelam
Why: The LTTE fought for a separate Tamil state called Tamil Eelam.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not names of the demanded state.
Key point: The demand for Eelam drove a long civil war.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Amendment shielding the PM's election from courts
questions.question: During the Emergency, an amendment declared that the election of which office-holders could not be challenged in court?
options: A) Chief Ministers and the Governors of States
B) Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts
C) Members of the Planning Commission of India
D) The Prime Minister, President and Vice-President
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Prime Minister, President and Vice-President
Why: An amendment declared that elections of the Prime Minister, President and Vice-President could not be challenged in court.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) were not covered by this amendment.
Key point: The amendment was a response to the Allahabad verdict.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why developing countries criticise the WTO
questions.question: Why is the WTO often criticised by developing countries?
options: A) Major economic powers dominate the making of its rules.
B) It refuses to deal with any questions of trade at all.
C) It is controlled entirely by the UN General Assembly.
D) It forbids all its members from exporting goods.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Major economic powers dominate the making of its rules.
Why: Critics say the US, the EU and Japan have managed to make WTO rules that serve their interests.
Why not the others:
(B) Trade is its main concern.
(C) The WTO is not controlled by the General Assembly.
(D) It promotes trade.
Key point: Unequal power shapes global trade rules.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: South Asia, 1977–2009, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) India sends a peacekeeping force to Sri Lanka
(B) General Zia-ul-Haq takes power in Pakistan
(C) The LTTE is defeated in Sri Lanka
(D) SAARC members sign the SAFTA agreement
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Why: (B) Zia took power in 1977. (A) The peacekeeping force was sent in 1987. (D) SAFTA was signed in 2004. (C) The LTTE was defeated in 2009.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts 1987 before 1977. Option (C) puts SAFTA before 1987. Option (D) puts 2009 before 2004.
Key point: 1977 → 1987 → 2004 → 2009.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Factions and coalitions of the 1960s
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Congress (R)
(B) Congress (O)
(C) Kamaraj Plan
(D) Samyukta Vidhayak Dal

List-II
(I) Senior leaders resigning from office to work for the party
(II) Indira Gandhi's faction after the split, the 'Requisitionists'
(III) Coalitions of non-Congress parties that ruled States after 1967
(IV) The faction led by the Syndicate after the split
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Congress (R) was Indira Gandhi's faction (II). Congress (O) was the Syndicate's faction (IV). Under the Kamaraj Plan, senior leaders resigned to work for the party (I). The SVD were non-Congress coalitions in the States (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the two Congress factions. Option (B) swaps Congress (O) and the Kamaraj Plan. Option (C) swaps the Kamaraj Plan and the SVD.
Key point: The 1960s saw the Congress divided and challenged.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Language movements before reorganisation
questions.question:
Match List-I (Movement) with List-II (Demand).

List-I
(A) Vishalandhra
(B) Mahagujarat
(C) Samyukta Maharashtra
(D) Punjabi Suba

List-II
(I) A State for Punjabi speakers
(II) A State for Gujarati speakers
(III) A State for Telugu speakers out of Madras
(IV) A State for Marathi speakers
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Vishalandhra sought a Telugu State (III). Mahagujarat sought a Gujarati State (II). Samyukta Maharashtra sought a Marathi State (IV). Punjabi Suba sought a Punjabi State (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Vishalandhra and Mahagujarat. Option (C) swaps Mahagujarat and Samyukta Maharashtra. Option (D) swaps Samyukta Maharashtra and Punjabi Suba.
Key point: Language movements reshaped the map of India.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Courts and amendments, 1973–1978, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Parliament passes the 42nd Amendment
(B) Parliament passes the 44th Amendment
(C) The Allahabad High Court sets aside Indira Gandhi's election
(D) Three senior judges are superseded in the appointment of the Chief Justice
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (D), (C), (A), (B)
Why: (D) The supersession took place in 1973. (C) The Allahabad verdict came in June 1975. (A) The 42nd Amendment was passed in 1976. (B) The 44th Amendment followed in 1978.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Allahabad verdict before the supersession. Option (B) puts the 44th Amendment before the 42nd. Option (D) puts the 42nd Amendment before the Allahabad verdict.
Key point: 1973 → 1975 → 1976 → 1978.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Background to the 1967 election
questions.question: Which of the following formed the background to the fourth general election of 1967?
options: A) Drought, food shortages, devaluation and rising prices
B) A sudden boom in exports and very low inflation
C) The end of the Emergency and the release of leaders
D) The completion of the Green Revolution across India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Drought, food shortages, devaluation and rising prices
Why: Monsoon failure, drought, falling farm output, food shortages, devaluation of the rupee and inflation created an economic crisis.
Why not the others:
(B) The economy was in crisis.
(C) The Emergency came in 1975.
(D) The Green Revolution was only beginning.
Key point: Economic hardship turned voters against the Congress.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Caste and religion in politics, 1978–1995, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) BAMCEF is formed
(B) Parliament passes the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act
(C) The BSP forms a government in Uttar Pradesh for the first time
(D) The Mandal Commission submits its report
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (D), (B), (C)
Why: (A) BAMCEF was formed in 1978. (D) The Mandal report came in 1980. (B) The Muslim Women Act was passed in 1986. (C) The BSP formed its first UP government in 1995.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Mandal report before BAMCEF. Option (B) puts the BSP government before the Act. Option (C) puts the Act before the Mandal report.
Key point: 1978 → 1980 → 1986 → 1995.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: What left critics say about globalisation
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Globalisation has provoked strong criticism. Critics on the left argue that it makes the rich richer and the poor poorer, both within countries and between them. They point out that when the state withdraws from welfare, the poorest lose the protection they once had. Others worry that local traditions and ways of life will be swamped by outside influences. Yet most movements of resistance do not reject global contacts altogether. What they oppose is a particular programme of globalisation, one that they see as driven by powerful states and corporations for their own benefit. Interestingly, these movements make full use of the tools that globalisation itself has created. Activists in different countries share ideas over the internet, coordinate protests across borders and meet at international gatherings. The World Social Forum, which first met in 2001, is one such gathering. It is not a political party and does not contest elections; rather, it is an open meeting place where human rights activists, environmentalists, labour groups, youth and women's organisations discuss alternatives. In this sense, the resistance to globalisation has itself become global.

Question: According to the passage, critics on the left argue that globalisation:
options: A) makes the rich richer and the poor poorer
B) ends poverty within a single generation
C) strengthens the welfare role of the state
D) affects only the developed countries
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) makes the rich richer and the poor poorer
Why: The passage says left critics argue that globalisation makes the rich richer and the poor poorer.
Why not the others:
(B) The critics say the opposite.
(C) The passage says the state withdraws from welfare.
(D) The passage speaks of effects within and between all countries.
Key point: Inequality is the core of the left critique.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: What the resistance movements actually oppose
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: What, according to the passage, do most movements of resistance oppose?
options: A) Every kind of contact between countries
B) The use of the internet for any purpose
C) A particular programme of globalisation
D) The existence of international gatherings
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A particular programme of globalisation
Why: The passage says the movements do not reject global contacts but oppose a particular programme driven by powerful states and corporations.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage says they do not reject global contacts.
(B) They use the internet themselves.
(D) They hold international gatherings themselves.
Key point: Resistance targets a specific kind of globalisation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: How resisters use globalisation's own tools
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: How, according to the passage, do resistance movements make use of globalisation?
options: A) By setting up their own multinational companies
B) By asking the WTO to fund their protests
C) By forming a single world government of activists
D) By sharing ideas online and organising across borders
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) By sharing ideas online and organising across borders
Why: The passage says activists share ideas over the internet, coordinate protests across borders and meet internationally.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not mentioned in the passage.
Key point: Technology links movements across the world.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Statement about the World Social Forum at odds with the passage
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Which of the following statements is at odds with the passage?
options: A) The World Social Forum first met in 2001.
B) The World Social Forum is a party that contests elections.
C) Environmentalists and labour groups take part in the Forum.
D) The Forum is a place to discuss alternatives to the present order.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The World Social Forum is a party that contests elections.
Why: The passage says the Forum is not a political party and does not contest elections, so (B) contradicts it.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are each stated in the passage.
Key point: The WSF is an open meeting place, not a party.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: What the passage means by 'resistance has become global'
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Globalisation has provoked strong criticism. Critics on the left argue that it makes the rich richer and the poor poorer, both within countries and between them. They point out that when the state withdraws from welfare, the poorest lose the protection they once had. Others worry that local traditions and ways of life will be swamped by outside influences. What they oppose is a particular programme of globalisation, one that they see as driven by powerful states and corporations for their own benefit. It is not a political party and does not contest elections; rather, it is an open meeting place where human rights activists, environmentalists, labour groups, youth and women's organisations discuss alternatives. In this sense, the resistance to globalisation has itself become global.

Question: What does the passage suggest when it says that resistance to globalisation 'has itself become global'?
options: A) Resistance has been taken over by the governments of rich countries.
B) The movements now support every policy of the big corporations.
C) Resistance has ended because globalisation has stopped spreading.
D) Opponents of globalisation now work together across many countries.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Opponents of globalisation now work together across many countries.
Why: The passage describes activists linking up across borders through the internet and gatherings like the WSF, so their resistance is international.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage says nothing of governments taking over.
(B) The movements oppose the corporate-driven programme.
(C) The passage does not say globalisation has stopped.
Key point: The critics of globalisation use its own networks.
